opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. That's a question I've thought about quite a bit, because my view has really shifted over the years.

When I started out in computer vision, I was very drawn to elegant formulations: a clean objective function, a nice probabilistic model, maybe a convex relaxation with a provable guarantee. There was a sense that if the math was beautiful, the method was probably right. A lot of us in that generation were trained that way. You'd write a paper, and much of the satisfaction came from the derivation itself.

Then deep learning arrived, and a lot of that intuition got challenged. Some of the methods that worked best weren't the most mathematically elegant ones. Often they were simple, even a bit crude, but they scaled. GANs are an interesting example for me. The original idea, a two-player game between a generator and a discriminator, is beautiful. But making GANs actually work involved many engineering tricks, normalization choices, architecture details, and training heuristics. And the theory often came after the empirical success, not before.

So today I'd say beauty has moved for me. It's less about the elegance of a single equation and more about the elegance of a principle that scales: a simple idea that keeps getting better as you add more data, more compute, and a bigger model. Diffusion models and the large-scale training behind world foundation models have that quality. The core formulation is quite clean, and its real beauty shows when you see how far it can go.

I still appreciate mathematical beauty, and it's a very useful guide for building intuition and deciding which direction to explore. But I've become more humble about it. Nature and data have a way of telling you what really matters. Now I think the most beautiful research combines a simple, principled idea with the engineering discipline to push it to scale and see what emerges.

r001.rationale: The response mentions elegant formulations and provable guarantees, but does not say that assumptions used to prove optimization bounds distance computer vision research from reality.

r002.rationale: The response describes valuing scalable principles, empirical results, and engineering more than equation-level elegance. It does not clearly state a shift toward prioritizing the essence of the practical problem being addressed.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. That's a question I think about more than I expected to when I started.

When I was doing my PhD, beauty in research meant elegance of formulation. A clean objective function, a proof that something converges, a method you could write on a single whiteboard and explain in ten minutes. That was the aesthetic I was trained in, and honestly it was the aesthetic that got papers accepted. If your method had too many moving parts, reviewers would ask why you needed them. The implicit assumption was that the right idea should be simple.

Then around the time of GANs, and later with diffusion and large language models, something shifted for me. The things that actually worked often did not look beautiful at first. GAN training was a mess. There were dozens of tricks, and nobody fully understood which ones mattered. Scaling laws, when they appeared, felt almost offensive to a certain kind of mathematical taste. You are telling me the answer is just more data and more compute? Where is the insight?

But I came to see that there is a different kind of beauty there, and it took me a while to recognize it. The beauty is not in the equation. It is in the fact that a very simple recipe, applied at scale, produces behavior that nobody designed. When we train a video model and it learns that water reflects light, that objects persist when they go behind something, that shadows follow the sun, no one wrote those rules down. The physics emerges from a prediction objective. To me that is more profound than any closed-form solution I ever derived. The elegance moved from the method to the phenomenon.

I also think my earlier view was a bit of a trap. When you optimize for a beautiful formulation, you tend to solve problems that admit beautiful formulations. The real world does not. Building world models for robotics or autonomous systems means dealing with enormous messiness, and insisting on elegance too early means you never engage with the actual problem.

So now I would say I still care deeply about beauty, but my definition changed. Early on, beauty was about compression of the idea. Now I think of it more as compression of reality. A model that captures how the world behaves in a way we can build on, that is beautiful to me, even if the training pipeline has a thousand engineering decisions inside it. The mathematics is still there, it is just hiding in a different place.

r001.rationale: The response says elegant formulations can keep research from engaging with real-world messiness, but it does not mention assumptions for provable optimization bounds or computer vision research.

r002.rationale: The response clearly describes a shift from valuing elegant formulations to valuing models that capture real-world behavior and address practical problems.

astra-6.text:
I think I’ve become less attached to the idea that a beautiful mathematical formulation must lead to a useful result. You can have something very elegant on paper, but when you put it into a system and work with real data, the assumptions may not hold.

That doesn’t make mathematics less important. What I appreciate more now is when the mathematics helps us understand why something works, where it fails, and what to try next. A simple idea that explains an unexpected result can be just as beautiful as a sophisticated derivation.

So my view has broadened. The beauty is in the connection between the theory and the behavior you actually observe.

r001.rationale: The response says assumptions may not hold with real data, but does not connect them to proving optimization bounds or to computer vision research becoming distant from reality.

r002.rationale: The response describes valuing theory’s connection to observed behavior, but does not clearly state a shift toward prioritizing the essence of the practical problem.

sol-6.1.text:
I think I’ve become less attached to elegance on paper and more interested in the connection between an idea and what it lets us discover. A formulation can be beautiful, but if it depends on assumptions that don’t survive contact with the problem, that beauty has limits.

What I find especially beautiful now is when a simple principle explains something surprising in a complicated system. You observe a behavior, you struggle to understand it, and then a mathematical perspective makes several pieces fall into place. It doesn’t have to explain everything. Sometimes just revealing the right question is a beautiful contribution.

So I still value elegance, but I see it more as a guide than a requirement. The experiments can challenge our intuition, and that tension can lead to better mathematics.
